title: Checkpoint: Democracy
objective: After this level you can explain how democracies share power and hold leaders to account.
summary: Churchill: democracy is the worst form of government except all the others. Democracies share power (parliaments, branches, checks) and hold leaders to account (confidence votes, press, speech).

cards.headline: Churchill called democracy the worst form of government. Then came "except".
cards.body: On 11 November 1947, Winston Churchill told the House of Commons: "it has been said that democracy is the worst form of Government except all those other forms that have been tried from time to time."

cards.headline: Not perfect, and not pretending
cards.body: In the same remarks Churchill said no one pretends democracy is perfect or all-wise. And "it has been said" gives the game away: he was repeating a saying already going around, not coining it. This chapter has been a tour of that "except": the ways democracies avoid trusting anyone with everything, from a king bound by Magna Carta to Montesquieu's warning that united powers leave no liberty.

items.label: Share power
points: Parliaments make laws and control taxes
Separate branches that can block each other

items.label: Hold leaders to account
points: A free press, free expression and peaceful assembly

cards.headline: From a Greek word to a working machine
cards.body: The chapter began with demokratia, rule by the people, and Lincoln's government of, by and for the people. Everything since is machinery for making that phrase true: parliaments that talk before they decide, prime ministers who can lose parliament's confidence, presidents elected for fixed terms, parties that organize voters and opposition, and reporters in the gallery.

mascot.line: Ten levels on who holds power and who keeps an eye on them. Nicely done.

cards.headline: Chapter 3 complete
learned: Churchill: the worst form, except all the others
Democracies share power: parliaments, branches, checks
They hold leaders to account: confidence votes, courts
A free press and free speech keep people informed

options.rationale: He defended democracy against the alternatives.

questions.prompt: Democracy checkpoint: who warned that there is no liberty when legislative and executive powers are united?

options.label: Winston Churchill
options.rationale: Churchill's line was about democracy and the alternatives.

options.label: Abraham Lincoln
options.rationale: Lincoln's line was government of, by and for the people.

questions.explanation: Montesquieu, in The Spirit of Laws, warned that uniting legislative and executive power leaves no liberty.

questions.prompt: Democracy checkpoint: Britain's 1979 no-confidence vote and South Korea's 2016 impeachment were both examples of what?

options.label: Courts overruling a new law
options.rationale: Both began with lawmakers acting on a leader.

options.label: Leaders dissolving parliament
options.rationale: The checks ran the other way: lawmakers on leaders.

questions.explanation: In 1979 the Commons voted no confidence in Callaghan's government; in 2016 South Korea's National Assembly impeached President Park.

questions.prompt: Democracy checkpoint: Lincoln's "government ... by the people" echoes which Level 7 thinker's view that government rests on the consent of the governed?

options.label: Thomas Hobbes
options.rationale: Hobbes handed power to a sovereign in exchange for protection.

options.label: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
options.rationale: Rousseau's idea was the general will.

options.label: Max Weber
options.rationale: Weber classified authority; consent of the governed is Locke's phrase.

questions.explanation: For Locke, government gets its legitimacy from the consent of the governed: the people are the source of authority.
